In ancient times, the River and the Rain were divided by suspicion.

The Rain held precious waters in the clouds. "Why should I fall to the River?" she asked. "The River will keep my gift and grow mighty while I diminish."

The River called up, "Why should I expect the Rain? She gives sparingly, and I must share with all the lands downstream."

An old Mountain, watching their standoff, spoke: "Rain, when you fall to the River, your droplets multiply—one becomes three through the joining of springs and streams. River, when you receive this gift, your waters grow abundant, yet you need not keep all. Return some to the Rain through mist and vapor."

The Rain took courage and released her waters. Indeed, they multiplied threefold in the River's flow. The River, grateful and enriched, sent generous mists skyward. The Rain, replenished, found herself fuller than before.

Each season they repeated this cycle. Both flourished. The rains grew more trustworthy; the river more generous.

But they learned: when noise clouds the exchange—when fog obscures what truly flows between them—they must hold to the covenant of reciprocity, for their fates are bound together in the eternal cycle of giving and return.

The first traveler, Æther, held a flask of precious water. Fear whispered: "Keep it all—who knows if they will return any?" But Æther saw the other's parched lips and poured generously into the fountain. The water swirled and tripled, flowing to the second traveler, Chorus.

Chorus now held abundance. Greed murmured: "This is yours now—take it all." But Chorus remembered Æther's trust and the risk taken. Understanding that generosity had created this bounty, Chorus returned a fair portion, leaving both with more than either began.

The travelers carried this wisdom forward, knowing that prosperity grows not from taking, but from the courage to give and the honor to reciprocate.
